title: Who carried the most
subtitle: Statistics queries that turn a night of traffic into a shortlist
intro: Odalys needs a one-page brief for the board at 07:00, not a thousand rows. Statistics queries are how you compress a night into a table: group by something, calculate per group, sort, cut. You have used each piece; this chapter is about composing them on purpose.
concepts: limit cuts the output, not the search
recap: Sum a numeric field per group, sort it and cut the list with limit
Read the span of an activity from min and max on the timestamp
Say what limit keeps when the order flips, and why a quiet machine is not a clean one
Calculate two or three outcomes per row and group by one or two keys
Choose count or count_distinct from the question you were asked, and read the two together

missions.title: Top talkers by bytes sent
missions.beat: Rank every machine on the pier by how much it sent out tonight. Five rows, biggest first. The board can read five rows.
missions.question: Which machine sent the most data out, and by how much?

concept.title: limit cuts the output, not the search
concept.text: limit 5 returns five rows after grouping, calculating and sorting are done. It does not scan five events. The order section is what decides which five you see, so an order with the wrong direction gives you the five smallest.

explain.meaning: Add up the numeric field within each group.
Keep the first five rows of the sorted result.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $bytes_out desc
limit:
  5
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $bytes_out desc
limit:
  5
hints: Run it. Compare the first row with the second.
Change desc to asc and run again: the limit now keeps the five quietest machines.
AUTOMATION-01 sent about 48 million bytes. The next machine sent under two million.

answer.prompt: Which hostname is in the first row?

call.prompt: The first row's total is roughly 27 times the second row's. What should the brief say?

options.label: The playout PC streams audio all night, so a large outbound total from it is expected and not worth a line
The playout PC is the outlier: one connection at 02:10 accounts for almost all of it
Every machine in the top five should be reimaged before the morning news, since all of them sent data out

call.why: The playout PC's normal streaming is inbound (received bytes). Outbound volume on that scale from that machine is new tonight, and you already know the connection that caused it.

missions.clue: AUTOMATION-01, 48,345,375 bytes out. Studio A, in second place, is under two million and that is a night of normal use. One machine, one connection, one spreadsheet.

logIt.prompt: Log the upload as evidence. Time: 02:10. Observation: AUTOMATION-01 sent 48,345,375 bytes tonight; one NETWORK_CONNECTION at 02:10:33 carried 48,230,112 of them to 203.0.113.44 on port 443, five minutes after donors_export.zip was written. Records: that connection. State size, direction, destination and time; what the stream contained is inference.

missions.caveat: Sum ignores nothing. A single misparsed byte field can dominate a total; click into the biggest group before you quote it.

missions.title: First and last
missions.beat: The board will ask when it started and when it stopped. Those are the earliest and latest beacon lookups, and a statistics query can hand them to you as two columns: the minimum and maximum timestamp per machine.
missions.question: When did AUTOMATION-01 first and last look up the beacon name?

concept.title: min and max on a timestamp are first and last
concept.text: metadata.event_timestamp.seconds is a number, seconds since 1970 in UTC. min of it in a group is the earliest event; max is the latest. The desk shows those cells as clock times with the raw seconds beside them, because that is how you would read them in a brief. Two aggregates in one query give you the span of an activity without scrolling to either end of a table.

explain.meaning: The earliest timestamp in each group.
The latest. Together they are the span.
One row per machine that asked for the name. Only one did.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = "cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $first = ___(metadata.event_timestamp.seconds)
  $last = max(metadata.event_timestamp.seconds)
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = "cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $first = min(metadata.event_timestamp.seconds)
  $last = max(metadata.event_timestamp.seconds)
hints: The earliest time in a group is its smallest number. The aggregate that returns the smallest value is the opposite of max.
Fill the gap with min.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
network.dns.questions.name = "cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $first = min(metadata.event_timestamp.seconds)
  $last = max(metadata.event_timestamp.seconds)

answer.prompt: What clock time is in the $first column for AUTOMATION-01 (HH:MM, UTC)?

call.prompt: The span runs from a few minutes after the task was created until a few minutes before the data ends. What should the brief say about whether it stopped?

options.label: That the activity ended at the last lookup, since a max is a max and the brief can give the board a stop time
That it was still running when the data ends; the latest lookup is the edge of the window, not the end of the behaviour
That it ran for exactly the span between the two times, and the number of lookups divided by that span is the proof it was automated

call.why: A maximum at the edge of the time range means the activity outlived the data. The task is still scheduled until someone removes it; that is a Contain item, not a stop time.

missions.clue: First lookup 19:40:05, four minutes after the task was created. Last lookup 05:50:06, ten minutes before the data ends. Nothing in between stopped it, and nothing in the data says it has stopped now.

logIt.prompt: Add two Timeline entries if you like; one is required. Time: 05:50. Fact: AUTOMATION-01's last lookup of cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example in the data is at 05:50:06; the first was at 19:40:05. The task was still scheduled when the data ends. Evidence ref: the # of your cadence evidence.

missions.caveat: Google exposes timestamp helpers (timestamp.get_hour and friends) that this trainer does not run. In a tenant you would format the span with those rather than reading raw seconds.

missions.title: The quiet end of the list
missions.beat: Flip the sort. Rank the machines by connection count from fewest to most and keep three. The point is not the quiet machines; the point is what limit keeps when the order changes, and whether quiet means clean.
missions.question: Which three machines made the fewest connections tonight?

concept.title: order decides what limit keeps
concept.text: limit takes the first rows of the sorted table. With desc, it keeps the biggest; with asc, the smallest; with no order section at all, it keeps whatever came first in key order, which is rarely what you meant. Always read the order line before you trust a limited table. And a quiet machine is not a clean one: the second-quietest tonight is the one that clicked the link.

explain.meaning: Smallest first. asc is the default, so writing just $connections does the same thing; writing it out says what you meant.
Three rows after sorting. Change asc to desc and the same limit keeps the three busiest.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $connections ___
limit:
  3
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $connections asc
limit:
  3
hints: You want the smallest counts first. The direction word is the opposite of desc.
Fill the gap with asc.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  principal.hostname
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
order:
  $connections asc
limit:
  3

answer.prompt: Which hostname is in the first row?

call.prompt: The victim's desk, PLEDGE-DESK-02, is in your bottom three. A colleague says the quiet machines can be ruled out of the brief. What do you say?

options.label: Agree; low volume means low exposure, and the brief has enough to cover without listing machines that barely used the network
Disagree; two of that desk's few connections are the click and the form post, so a short list is where the quiet, decisive events hide
Agree in part; keep PLEDGE-DESK-02 only because Hal owns it, since a treasurer's machine is politically sensitive whatever the logs say

call.why: Volume ranks noise. The connection that started the night was one of twenty-one on a quiet desk. A sort is a way of reading the table, not a filter on what matters.

missions.clue: Fewest connections: ENG-SHOP-01 with eighteen, PLEDGE-DESK-02 with twenty-one, NEWSROOM-03 with forty-one. The second-quietest machine on the pier is where the password left. Flip to desc and the top row is the playout PC, where it was used.

logIt.prompt: Log a Gap: connection counts and byte totals come from one sensor; a quiet machine may be quiet because it was lightly logged, not lightly used, and the dataset has no proxy or endpoint network log to cross-check. Why it matters: ENG-SHOP-01 and PLEDGE-DESK-02 rank quietest and one of them is the victim desk; ranking by volume cannot clear a machine.

missions.caveat: Google's order section accepts several outcomes and a direction for each. A tie on the first key is broken by the next; with no further key the order of tied rows is not guaranteed.

missions.title: Where the playout PC was talking
missions.beat: Narrow to AUTOMATION-01 and break its connections down by destination address and port. Two calculations per row this time: how many connections, and how many bytes.
missions.question: How many connections did AUTOMATION-01 make to 203.0.113.44 on port 443?

concept.title: Two outcomes in one query
concept.text: An outcome section can hold several calculations; each becomes a column. Grouping by two keys, address and port, gives one row per pair. This is the shape of most hunting dashboards.

explain.meaning: Two grouping keys separated by a comma. One row per distinct combination.
Two outcomes, one per line, each with its own name.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
principal.hostname = "AUTOMATION-01"
match:
  target.ip, ___
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $connections desc
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
principal.hostname = "AUTOMATION-01"
match:
  target.ip, target.port
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $connections desc
hints: The second grouping key is the destination port.
match: target.ip, target.port

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
principal.hostname = "AUTOMATION-01"
match:
  target.ip, target.port
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $connections desc

call.prompt: Compare the two rows: the streaming CDN at 192.0.2.120 with about 60 KB sent, and the attacker address with 48 MB sent, at similar connection counts. Which comparison matters more?

options.label: Connection count; the attacker row has more connections, so it is the busier of the two and the one to lead with
Neither; both rows are port 443, so both are ordinary web traffic for a playout PC that streams all night
Bytes per destination; the CDN sends almost nothing out while the attacker address received 48 MB

call.why: Counts describe rhythm; bytes describe payload. Both rows look beacon-like by count, but only one carried a file.

missions.clue: Two destinations all night. The streaming CDN: 40 connections, 59 KB out, which is a player saying hello. The attacker address: 63 connections, 48 MB out. Sixty-two were heartbeats. One was the donor list.

logIt.prompt: Add a Timeline entry. Time: 02:10. Fact: 48 MB left AUTOMATION-01 for 203.0.113.44 on port 443, the one connection of 63 to that address that carried a payload. Evidence ref: your upload evidence. For contrast, the CDN at 192.0.2.120 took 40 connections and 59 KB all night.

missions.caveat: Try removing order and see the rows come back in key order. The data is the same; only the reading changes.

missions.title: Three numbers per destination
missions.beat: One table for the board: every destination address tonight, with how many connections reached it, how many different machines made them, and how many bytes went out. Three calculations per row. Read the top row against the rest.
missions.question: How many different machines connected to the attacker address, and how does its row compare with the station's normal services?

concept.title: Three outcomes, three questions
concept.text: count answers "how often". count_distinct on the host answers "how widely". sum on the bytes answers "how much". A benign service scores high on the first two and low on the third: many machines, many connections, little sent. The attacker address scores the other way: two machines, a clock's worth of connections, and almost everything the pier sent out tonight.

explain.meaning: Three outcomes, three columns. Each has its own name.
Sorted by what left the building.

missions.starter:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  target.ip
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
  $hosts = count_distinct(principal.hostname)
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $bytes_out desc
missions.reference:
metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_CONNECTION"
match:
  target.ip
outcome:
  $connections = count(metadata.id)
  $hosts = count_distinct(principal.hostname)
  $bytes_out = sum(network.sent_bytes)
order:
  $bytes_out desc
hints: Run it. Read the top row, then read the $hosts column down the whole table.
Every ordinary service was reached by six or seven machines. One address was reached by fewer.
The attacker address: 65 connections, two hosts (PLEDGE-DESK-02 and AUTOMATION-01), about 48 million bytes out. Every other row: six or seven hosts, about a million bytes or less.

call.prompt: The CDN row has more connections than the attacker row and three times as many hosts. The attacker row has forty times the bytes out. Which column should lead the brief?

options.label: Connections; it is the most direct measure of activity and the board understands a count better than a byte total
Bytes out, with the host count beside it: almost everything the pier sent out went to one address that only two machines ever reached
Hosts; the fewer machines that reached an address, the more targeted it is, so the host count alone ranks the threat

call.why: One column ranks; the others explain. Bytes out puts the attacker address first, and the host count says why that is strange for an address that busy.

missions.clue: Eight destinations. Seven of them: six or seven machines each, a million bytes or less sent. One of them: two machines, 65 connections, 48 million bytes. The table is the brief.

logIt.prompt: Log the destination table as evidence. Time: the whole night as a range. Observation: 203.0.113.44 received 65 connections from two hosts (PLEDGE-DESK-02 and AUTOMATION-01) and about 48 million bytes; every other destination was reached by six or seven hosts and received about a million bytes or less. Records: the 02:10 upload, which carries almost all of those bytes. Where to find it: a three-outcome statistics query grouped by target.ip.

missions.caveat: Real destination tables run to thousands of rows. The three-column shape still works; add a limit and an order on the column that answers your question.

missions.title: How many, how many different
missions.beat: Last one for the brief. The playout PC asked DNS for names all night. Odalys wants two numbers in one line: how many lookups it made, and how many different names it asked for. Build both outcomes in one query, no match section.
missions.question: How many DNS lookups did AUTOMATION-01 make tonight, and for how many different names?

concept.title: count and count_distinct on the same field
concept.text: count counts events. count_distinct counts different values. On a field that repeats, the two numbers diverge, and the gap between them is the story: a hundred lookups for two names is a machine on a schedule, not a person browsing. Put both in one outcome section and the brief gets its sentence from one row.

hints: Filter DNS events from AUTOMATION-01, then an outcome section with two lines: count of the name field, and count_distinct of the same field. No match section gives one summary row.

outcome:
  $lookups = count(network.dns.questions.name)
  $names = count_distinct(network.dns.questions.name) under the two filter lines.

metadata.event_type = "NETWORK_DNS"
principal.hostname = "AUTOMATION-01"
outcome:
  $lookups = count(network.dns.questions.name)
  $names = count_distinct(network.dns.questions.name)

answer.prompt: What is your count (not count_distinct) value?

call.prompt: Over a hundred lookups for exactly two names. One is the streaming CDN the playout PC has always used. What is the right sentence for the brief?

options.label: The playout PC resolved two names all night, one of them the station's own CDN and the other the lookalike's content host, every ten minutes from 19:40
The playout PC's DNS traffic is normal for a machine that streams, since two names is a very small set and the count is in line with a busy night
The playout PC made over a hundred suspicious DNS requests, which is the number the board should hear first

call.why: The count alone alarms and the distinct count alone reassures. Together, with the names, they describe exactly what happened: one expected name and one that was not, on a clock.

missions.clue: A hundred and two lookups, two names: streaming.tunecast.example, which the playout PC has always asked for, and cdn-sync.pier9-partners.example, which it started asking for at 19:40 and never stopped. A machine with a two-name vocabulary, half of it borrowed.

logIt.prompt: Write a Recover item: rebuild AUTOMATION-01 from a known-good image, restore the playout schedule and verify the 06:30 news airs, then confirm the rebuilt machine resolves only its expected names (streaming.tunecast.example and the vendor hosts) over a full day. Answers: your cadence evidence and your PledgeSync folder evidence. Owner role: volunteer engineer. Urgency: today.

missions.caveat: count(field) in Google counts events where the field is present; count(metadata.id) counts every event. On a field every event carries they agree, as here.

missions.title: How many inboxes got the lure?
missions.beat: Last question for the brief: how many distinct mailboxes received the sponsor-portal lure? You know the exact sender address. Build the count yourself.
missions.question: How many different recipients did the lookalike sender reach?

concept.title: count versus count_distinct
concept.text: count tells you how many messages. count_distinct on the recipient tells you how many different inboxes. The two differ the moment one person is mailed twice. Choose the one that matches the question you were asked.

hints: Filter on the exact sender address, then use an outcome that counts distinct recipient addresses. No match section is needed for one overall number.
Under the sender filter, add an outcome section with $recipients = count_distinct(network.email.to).

network.email.from = "sponsorships@pier9-partners.example"
outcome:
  $recipients = count_distinct(network.email.to)

answer.prompt: What is the value of your distinct-recipient count?

call.prompt: The lure reached Hal, Odalys and the shared pledge-desk mailbox. Only Hal's machine resolved the domain. What goes in the brief?

options.label: Staff were targeted; one followed the link; the shared account's password is the likely loss and must be reset now
Hal caused the breach by clicking the link, and the brief should say so in those words so the board knows who to hold responsible
Odalys and the pledge desk are cleared because their machines never resolved the domain, so only Hal's inbox needs attention

call.why: Blame is not an action item; a password reset and a check of the other two inboxes are. Odalys and the desk did not click tonight, but the lure is still sitting there.

missions.clue: Three targets, one click, one shared password, one playout PC. The brief writes itself: phishing at 18:40, credential use from outside at 19:21, persistence at 19:35, staging at 02:05, exfiltration at 02:10, defacement on air at 03:10. Chapter 6 proves the timing.

logIt.prompt: Write an Eradicate item: reset the pledge-desk password now, end its sessions, and remove the lure from the two inboxes that did not click (odalys.reyes and the pledge-desk mailbox). Answers: your lure evidence and your burst evidence. Owner role: station manager or IT lead. Urgency: now. Blame is not an action item.

missions.caveat: If the gateway logged each recipient as a separate message, count and count_distinct agree. If it logged one message with a list, they would not. Know your source.
